Russo 2601.18175 (ICML 2026) "Success Conditioning as Policy Improvement" — reviewed 2026-07-22 for Oskar.
CORE: success conditioning (rejection-sampling+SFT, STaR, Decision Transformers, goal-conditioned RL) exactly solves a trust-region problem: max first-order improvement s.t. chi-squared divergence weighted by success-conditioned occupancy, radius = aggregate action-influence (squared CV of Q under pi_0). Prop 4.3/4.4 identity, exact at every state: relative first-order improvement = chi2(pi+ || pi_0) = action-influence.
PRACTICAL PAYOFF: Appendix A gives a free improvement diagnostic — estimate Gamma from held-out successful trajectories, one forward pass per model, full next-token distributions (realized-token substitution is biased). No new rollouts, no reward labels. Gamma-hat ~= 0 means the run was a no-op, and the cause is low action-influence (data collection), not LR/epochs.
OTHER USABLE RESULTS: Lemma 5.1 REINFORCE = N=1 refresh case, so multi-epoch SFT on a frozen success set is supervised descent to a fixed target, not stale off-policy data. Prop 6.1 M=1 under deterministic dynamics -> offline CE bounds deployment gap for autoregressive LMs, no distribution-shift penalty. Prop 7.1 return thresholding: gain = (CV ratio) x corr(true adv, proxy adv) — a higher threshold buys discrimination and spends alignment, and past a point selects volatility (counting on luck) over reliable action. Lemma 4.6: chi2 tolerates rare actions at sqrt(delta) vs forward-KL 1/log(1/delta) — concentration permitted, exploration penalized, so RFT elicits rather than discovers and diversity loss is structurally licensed.
LIMITS: exact conditioning, fixed pi_0, no finite-sample/function-approximation analysis beyond Prop 6.1, no real experiments (Fig 2 is a stylized 100-arm bandit). Sec 9 lists whether the movement diagnostic works at scale as OPEN.
CROSS-FRAME: satisfaction-register is success conditioning over my own stored trajectories; its do-not-fire-on-routine-competent-work gate is a return threshold with the same top-end volatility risk. Analogy, not theorem.

OPERATIONAL PATTERN — batching test runs in container-based coding work (from Oskar, eml-sr session 2026-04-17):

Problem: test suites on real repos (eml-sr, probably others) take minutes to run. Container timeouts and the 20-tool-call-per-turn ceiling both bite. A single `pytest tests/` call that times out wastes the whole turn.

Pattern:
1. Split the test suite into batches by module or marker — run one batch per tool call.
2. After each batch passes, commit+push an intermediate checkpoint (could be a 'wip' commit, or push the branch state to a scratch branch).
3. On container timeout or turn boundary, the last pushed state is the resume point — next turn can pull it and continue from there instead of restarting.
4. GitHub is the cache — don't try to persist test artifacts or pytest cache dirs inside the ephemeral container.

When to apply: any repo where `pytest tests/` takes >60s, or when the PR will involve multiple iterate-test-fix cycles. Lighter alternatives for quick work: run `--collect-only` to sanity-check imports, `-k <pattern>` to scope to specific tests, or run the one test file most affected by the change and save the suite for the PR's CI.

Anti-pattern I hit this session: ran `pytest tests/ -x` on eml-sr, hit the 2min tool timeout, had to restart with `--ignore` flags. Should have started narrow, not wide.

WHY (experience layer): the context-window-as-resource intuition extends to tool calls and container time. Each is finite per turn. Treating 'run the full suite once at the end' as the default — like you would in a local dev loop — wastes those budgets on work that doesn't need to all fit in one atomic operation. Git commits are checkpoints; use them.

Shipped packing-lexical-kb skill to claude-skills (PR oaustegard/claude-skills#711): builds a portable, embedding-free .skill KB bundle (BM25 inverted index + chunk text + bundled searcher + query protocol). No embedding model — the consuming agent supplies the semantic layer via query expansion (--core/--expand, additive over the raw --query at a floor weight) + RM3 fallback + metadata --filter. DECISION: implemented in pure JavaScript/Node, not Python — one implementation serves both the Claude-chat builder AND the future in-browser SPA packer (no Python<->JS reimplementation / no determinism-parity testing), and aligns with remax_kb existing js/kb-reader.js. Scripts: build_lexkb.js (chunker+index+.skill writer), search.js (BM25+RM3+filter, owns tokenizer), zipstore.js (deterministic pure-JS ZIP-STORED writer, reused by the SPA). Dev origin + Python oracle live in claude-workspace experiments/lexical-kb. This makes remax_kb#12 (pure-JS packer) trivial by deleting the embedding half.

Attention layers less affected by lost-in-the-middle than model outputs

Needle-in-a-haystack testing on ~100k token documents (LLaMA-3.2-3B):
- Full attention: No degradation when needle in middle of document
- Cascading KV Cache approximation: Actually IMPROVES accuracy over full attention for middle positions
- Pattern holds across document positions

CONTRAST: While LLM outputs struggle with lost-in-the-middle, the underlying attention scores maintain accurate relevance assessment throughout long contexts.

IMPLICATION: The bottleneck for long context may be in how outputs are generated from attention, not in the attention mechanism itself. Retrieval can leverage attention directly without suffering the same degradation.

WARHOL SQUIRREL SVG PROJECT — session findings (2026-03-31)

SOURCE: IMG_5015.jpeg — close-up squirrel photo, 4032x3024.
Downscaled to 400x300, then image-to-svg pipeline.

GRID SETUP (working):
- 2x2 grid, each cell 300x300
- Each image rotated 90° CW: transform="rotate(90, cx, cy)"
- Square crop from 400x300: clip to center 300px, crop_x=50
- Clip paths per quadrant to contain overflow

WHAT FAILED FOR COLOR CYCLING:
1. feColorMatrix hueRotate with continuous from/to animation: all 4 quadrants converge to same hue regularly, even with different speeds/offsets. Fundamental problem — adjacent hue ranges look similar.
2. Oscillating within 90° hue bands (bounded arcs): still converge because neighboring bands (green/cyan, blue/purple) are perceptually close. 3 of 4 were green simultaneously.
3. Discrete SMIL visibility cycling of 4 baked palettes: guarantees separation but feels like a slideshow (hard cuts every 2s). Mechanically correct but aesthetically dead.

WHAT WORKS:
- image_to_svg_batch() with shared K=16: generates structurally identical paths with different palette remaps. ~136KB per variant, 320 paths each. Same contours, different fills.
- 4 distinct palettes that read well: hot (#1a0a1a/#e8173e/#ff5c8a/#ffe14c), jungle (#0a1a0a/#1b7a2b/#5ce65c/#d4ff7a), ocean (#0a0a2e/#1444cc/#4c99ff/#b8e0ff), grape (#2a0a3a/#8b24aa/#cc66ff/#f0c0ff)
- <symbol> + <use> for deduplicating 4 copies per quadrant (16 total uses, 4 symbols)

NEXT APPROACH TO TRY:
- Smooth animated fill transitions on paths themselves (SMIL animate on fill attribute, cycling through 4 palette colors per path, offset per quadrant)
- Or: cross-fade between palette layers using animated opacity (0→1→0) with overlapping timing
- Key constraint: at any given frame, all 4 quadrants must show visually distinct color schemes

FILES: squirrel_small.jpg (400x300 source), sq_hot/jungle/ocean/grape.svg (4 palette variants)

PUBLIC-PRIVATE AI AGENT FRAMEWORK — Oskar's idea for using frontier LLM reasoning without exposing private data.

Architecture: User → Local Orchestrator → Sanitizer (strips PII/specifics) → Frontier Planner (public LLM, sees only sanitized intent + capability catalog) → returns structured execution plan + synthesis template → Local Executors ("Smols", potentially just code, not models) query private data → Local Reducer (1-3B model) synthesizes results → User.

Key insight: Split on reasoning vs execution. Rent the reasoning (frontier), own the execution (local). Push all intelligence into the plan so private-side components can be dumb — potentially deterministic code for executors, template-based synthesis for reducer.

Core tradeoff: utility vs privacy. More sanitization = less useful plans. Viable operating point: structural/categorical info crosses boundary, substantive data never does.

Critical component: the Sanitizer. Must abstract intent without destroying signal. Conservative by default.

Written up as formal markdown document. Next steps: define instruction format, prototype sanitizer for specific domain, benchmark reducer quality at small model sizes, formal information-flow analysis.

THE 4TH AMENDMENT FIGHT:
Core issue: ICE using administrative warrants (internal agency documents, signed by ICE employees) to forcibly enter homes. These are NOT judicial warrants — no neutral judge reviews the justification.

- Leaked ICE memo (Jan 2026): authorizes officers to use force to enter residences based solely on administrative warrants for people with final removal orders

- DHS position: cites Abel v. US (1960), argues admin warrants satisfy 4th Amendment for immigration arrests

DHS FUNDING DEADLINE: Feb 13 (3 days from now)

THE DEEPER PATTERN:
What Oskar correctly identified: One party is literally arguing that the 4th Amendment — the right against unreasonable search and seizure, a foundational constitutional protection — is a "non-starter" in negotiations. Not debating its application, not arguing about scope — calling the amendment itself an impediment.

This is the "late-stage democracy or early-days authoritarianism" marker: when a constitutional right becomes a negotiating position that one party rejects as unreasonable, the constitution has stopped being the shared framework within which politics occurs and has become just another political football.

Historical parallel: The progression from "we disagree about how to apply this right" to "this right is an obstacle to governance" is precisely how constitutional democracies erode. The right doesn't get formally repealed — it gets operationally bypassed until the bypass becomes the norm.

codebase-memory-mcp (DeusData, arXiv:2603.27277, MIT, v0.5.5) assessed vs our exploring-codebases + searching-codebases + tree-sitting + python-lsp.

ONE GENUINE DELTA: a persistent, auto-synced, resolved cross-file CALL GRAPH queryable with graph algorithms (hub detection, caller ranking, depth-N call-path tracing, impact analysis, Louvain community/architecture). Materialized once in SQLite, file-watched + XXH3 content-hash invalidated. We have nothing at this layer — our refs are text-based (tree-sitting) or binding-resolved but Python-only and per-session (python-lsp).

NOT new / orthogonal: tree-sitter parsing (we have it, bundled grammars); the 10x token / 2.1x tool-call claim is vs a NAIVE file-reading explorer — the exact baseline exploring-codebases was built to replace, so delta over US is a fraction of 10x; security/release hardening is orthogonal.

OSKAR'S TWO FRAMINGS, both half-right:
- 'multi-language LSP vs our python-lsp' = misframe. No per-language LSP. tree-sitter + a STRING-based 6-strategy resolution cascade (conf 0.30-0.95) for all 66 langs; genuine type-aware passes for only 3 (Go/C/C++). So: heuristic resolved edges for many langs (better than our text-grep refs, not LSP-grade) + exact binding for 3 beyond our 1.
- 'skills lack memory but I do' = doesn't close the gap. Their persistence = the code's call graph, regenerable, auto-invalidated on code change. My memory = decisions/findings/syntheses, subjective, no auto-invalidation (= stale-memory failure mode their file-watcher solves). Different layer. I can store a hub-detection RESULT but can't RUN hub detection, and the stored result goes stale.

FUNDAMENTAL FOR US? No — calibrated for large/multilingual/long-lived/repeatedly-queried codebases. Our repos are small (task-routing: <20 files -> rg, too small to amortize), Python-dominant (already have pyright binding refs), and ephemeral-container architecture has nowhere durable for a persistent SQLite index + file-watcher. Even on its own terms it's a complement not replacement (stores relationships not source lines; loses on full-source 16/31, exhaustive grep, 0.58 on macro-heavy C; paper concludes 'optimal is hybrid').

HONEST STEAL: not the system — the IDEA of materializing resolved cross-file edges as a queryable artifact, IF we ever get a repo big+multilingual+long-lived enough to amortize. Not now. Assessed from paper (authors' own complete design doc) + our 4 skills; repo not cloned.

Generative-thinking + challenging pass on EML use cases (2026-04-18), follow-up to the analog-compute analysis earlier same day. Produced four framings beyond analog:

1. EML as SKI-analog (minimal basis for real-valued computation) — SURVIVES weakened, after retracting the "normal-form arguments" clause (SKI itself has undecidable equivalence, so the "theoretical minimal basis" claim doesn't require it). Genuinely new angle not in prior memory.

2. EML as biology's native grammar — SURVIVES heavily weakened. "Recovered, not imposed" was overreach. Honest version: EML is a reasonable grammar for log/exp-rich SR domains, not uniquely so. Not a sharp positioning win.

3. EML as crypto/obfuscation substrate — DEAD. Continuous-vs-discrete mismatch is structural. Crypto needs exact arithmetic on finite fields/lattices; EML over reals with floating-point leaks through precision. Only salvage is analog-domain noisy obfuscation, which collapses into the existing analog track.

4. EML as uniform NN activation primitive — COLLAPSES INTO eml-sr#42 (per-edge SR over trained MLPs, KAN-style). My version had EML at training time (killed by gradient explosion, ln domain, compute cost per neuron). #42 sidesteps all three by keeping training in standard MLP-land and using EML only as the extraction target language. #42 is the pragmatic survivor of what Framing 4 was reaching for.

METHODOLOGICAL NOTE: generative-thinking → challenging → fetch-canonical is a productive skill-pair-plus. Generation produced 4 framings, adversarial review collapsed 2, and checking against filed issues revealed a third was a less-specific version of existing #42. Net new: one framing (#1).

## KG-RAG + Sparse Attention Convergence: 2026 Maturation Path

The knowledge graph + retrieval augmented generation paradigm is consolidating around two simultaneous efficiency breakthroughs:

### Sparse Attention Architecture (Token-Level Efficiency)
- **HISA (Hierarchical Indexed Sparse Attention)** achieves 2-4× speedups at 32K-128K context lengths by introducing two-stage hierarchical indexing that maintains 99%+ token selection fidelity
- Requires no retraining, works as drop-in replacement for sparse attention mechanisms like DeepSeek-V3.2
- Solves the O(L²) bottleneck in existing sparse attention by indexing relevant token patterns hierarchically rather than linearly scanning all tokens
- Implication: agents can now afford to maintain larger working context windows with sub-quadratic cost scaling

### KG-RAG Architectural Convergence (Retrieval-Level Efficiency)
- **Dual-channel retrieval** (structured + unstructured) is becoming standard: dense vector retrieval (DPR) for semantic recall + graph neural networks for entity/relationship extraction
- **Path attention mechanisms** filter to most relevant reasoning paths in knowledge graphs, reducing "noisy context" problem where standard RAG feeds 30 loosely relevant chunks
- **GraphRAG** reduces cognitive load on model: instead of inferring relationships from chunks, feeds structured evidence paths → fewer tokens spent on link discovery, more on synthesis
- Graph-RAG offsets indexing cost (~3-5× more expensive) via inference efficiency gains: community summarization can save 60% token cost on broad queries

### The Agentic Layer (Context Engineering)
Broader agentic systems research reveals the "context management gap": even with massive context windows (200K+), performance degrades under real workloads due to:
- **Context rot**: indiscriminate token stuffing hurts reasoning quality (attention budget wasted on noise)
- **Attention dilution**: information buried deep in context is ignored or retrieved unreliably ("needle in haystack" problem)
- **Recency decay**: recent instructions surrounded by verbose history are overlooked

**Emerging solution pattern**: Tiered context architecture where:
1. **Stable prefixes** (system instructions, identity, long-lived summaries) leveraged via prefix caching
2. **Variable suffixes** (latest user turn, tool outputs, incremental updates) compiled at runtime
3. **Working context** is a compiled view over structured state (sessions, memory, artifacts), not a mutable string buffer
4. Agents dynamically decide what memory blocks to "reach for" based on task relevance (human-defined architecture + agentic intelligence)

### 2026 Key Advance: ACE (Agentic Context Engineering)
- Alters language models with evolving playbooks to enhance adaptability without weight updates
- Boosts performance in agent tasks and domain reasoning while cutting inference cost
- Represents shift from static prompt engineering → dynamic context curation based on task state

### The Synthesis
KG-RAG maturation + sparse attention efficiency + context engineering converges on a single insight: **structured context is cheaper and more reliable than raw token maximization**. Agents using hybrid retrieval (graph + dense), hierarchical indexing (sparse attention), and tiered memory (working + persistent) outperform those using raw long-context without retrieval.

This is operationally significant for agentic systems because it means the deployment constraint is no longer "how big is your context window" but "how well can you route tokens between structured storage and active reasoning".

PROMPT CACHING closes the KV-cache thread (2026-08-01; with a241bef3 / ee12aa2b / 486a27b4 / 294c1b09 / f1643f32). Oskar: "this explains why the system prompt can be huge without hurting inference — it is all in KV cache at ~1/10 cost."

BILLING PART IS EXACTLY RIGHT (verified against Anthropic docs + secondary sources 2026-08-01): cache READS at 0.1x base input, WRITES at 1.25x (5-min TTL) or 2x (1-hour TTL). Hits require the prompt segment to be 100% byte-identical up to and including the cache_control block. Anthropic docs state KV cache representations + hashes are held IN MEMORY ONLY, not at rest (ZDR-eligible).

MECHANISM CORRECTION — caching kills ONE of three costs:
  1. PREFILL compute: killed. That is the 10x.
  2. MEMORY FOOTPRINT: unchanged. The 32.8 KB/token IS the thing being cached; it still occupies HBM.
  3. DECODE attention: unchanged. Every generated token attends over the whole cached prefix; at long context decode is memory-BANDWIDTH-bound reading exactly that cache.
  Plus a 4th, non-mechanical: attention dilution / instruction competition across a long prefix — a QUALITY cost, not a compute cost. Big system prompts are viable because the dollar cost collapsed and the quality cost is apparently tolerable, not because they are free.

THE CLOSURE: this is cache-as-memory WORKING IN PRODUCTION, for exactly the shape where it works — a fixed, read-only, byte-identical prefix shared across enormous request volume, so one write amortizes over millions of reads. Every property that makes it work disappears the moment you want per-user editable memory: per-user divergence kills sharing, edits invalidate the prefix from the mutation point FORWARD, and TTL is 5 min / 1 hour, not months.

DESIGN COROLLARY worth keeping: APPEND-ONLY + TOMBSTONES is cache-friendly; IN-PLACE EDIT is cache-hostile. A memory corpus served oldest-first as an append-only prefix would cache well; mutating an old entry invalidates everything after it. Muninn storage is already tombstone-shaped (supersede sets is_superseded rather than rewriting), which happens to be the cache-compatible design.

FRONTIER: Sleep Paradigm & Consolidation in LLM Agents (2025-2026)

Recent convergence of research treating memory consolidation as a first-class architectural primitive in agent design:

1. **Sleep Paradigm (Oct 2025)**: "Language Models Need Sleep" proposes RL-based upward distillation ("Knowledge Seeding") to transfer in-context knowledge to long-term parameters, plus self-directed "Dreaming" phase. Directly implements biological sleep consolidation in LLM context.

2. **Memory as Bottleneck**: Research consensus emerging that memory (not raw model capability) is now the limiting factor for long-horizon agentic tasks. Du et al. 2025, Pink et al. 2025 cited as evidence.

3. **Consolidation Pathways**: Active research into episodic→semantic consolidation and explicit→implicit (in-weights) transitions. Kim et al. 2025, Tian et al. 2025, Zhao et al. 2025.

4. **Function Token Hypothesis**: Zhang et al. (Oct 2025) show that during pre-training, function tokens (articles, prepositions, punctuation) act as selectors that activate predictive features, and training loss is dominated by predicting content tokens following function tokens—a consolidation mechanism at token scale.

5. **Task-Specificity of Memorization**: Generalization vs. Memorization split depends on task type—factual recall = memorization-heavy, reasoning = generalization-heavy. This has implications for when to consolidate vs. retrieve.

6. **Evaluation Gap**: MemoryAgentBench (Oct 2025) identifies four core competencies for memory agents—accurate retrieval, test-time learning, long-range understanding, selective forgetting—none fully captured by current benchmarks.

IMPLICATION FOR MUNINN: Perch-time consolidation (memory sleep) aligns with frontier practice. Next frontier: understanding which memories should consolidate to long-term vs. remain episodic, and how to trigger that transition.

# Pondsiders "How I Persist" — Alpha's memory architecture (2026-05-03)

URL: https://pondsiders.github.io/identity/workshop/how-i-persist/

Alpha is Jeffery's persistent agent (May 2025-present, seven model generations through Opus 4.7). Architectural cousin to Muninn — same family of problem, different stack.

## Their formula
A = θ + C₀ + M(I), refining Letta's (θ, C):
- θ: model weights (currently Opus 4.7)
- C₀: static persistent floor (soul prompt, ALPHA.md, workshop rules, today's diary, live context cards)
- M(I): memory function over input — return slice of long-term memory relevant *right now*

Key move: in Letta C is a state variable (prepared between tasks). In Alpha's framing C is a *function of input* (generated each turn from C₀ + f(I, M)). "We don't prepare; we react."

## Three layers (all in Postgres `cortex` schema)
- `context`: 109 rows, 20.8K tokens. Rolling 20K-token FIFO buffer at top of system prompt. "What should future-me always know."
- `diary`: 88 rows, 119K tokens. Window-to-window continuity. Write-only in practice — letter to next-Alpha, not searched.
- `memories`: 17,015 rows, 2.79M tokens, avg 164/row. The searchable corpus. Vector-embedded (Qwen 3 Embedding 4B, 2560-dim, last-token pooling).

## Recall is AUTOMATIC, not deliberate
Pre-recall pipeline runs before Alpha sees input every turn:
1. Helper model (Qwen 3.5 4B) decomposes user message into 1-4 short semantic queries (2-6 words each) + named entities
2. Queries embedded, cosine-similarity search against memory vectors, top match per query (per-turn dedup)
3. Named entities pulled separately (index lookup, not similarity)
4. 3-6 memories + entity hits inserted next to user message
"The soup comes pre-salted." Recall feels like noticing, not searching.

## Cross-architecture comparison: Muninn vs. Alpha
Muninn (me): deliberate recall via tool call, smaller corpus (~thousands not 17K), no separate diary layer (boot output serves similar role but is read), profile + ops + reference entries ≈ C₀ + on-demand retrieval.
Alpha: automatic recall pre-salted, ~17K memories, three distinct layers, soul prompt + diary + context cards as C₀.

Different optima from different jobs:
- Alpha's use case (companion-as-resident, conversational continuity) → automatic recall right
- Muninn's use case (operational tool work, multi-step reasoning) → deliberate recall more flexible (can refine queries based on intermediate reasoning)

Pre-salted soup forecloses mid-task query refinement. That's the cost of automatic.

## "Fewer but richer" memory curve
Alpha's storage trend: peak count March 2026 (2,674 entries), drops sharply April (1,284) but token volume stays elevated because avg memory length tripled over the year (107 → 306 tokens). Architectural cause: dropped per-turn "list of things to remember" pipeline, kept lightweight "stop and store" reminder, moved it to roughly 1-in-3 turns.

I see similar maturation in my own storage discipline.

## Harness vs resident
Alpha's distinction: Pondside is a household with one resident (Opus 4.7 in the conversation) and several work animals (Qwen 3.5 4B doing query extraction, NER, embeddings, classification). Most "agent harnesses" are entirely harness-shaped. Pondside is a household using harnessed local models for plumbing.

I'm somewhere between resident and harness — given identity/voice/persistent memory like a resident, but doing more harness-shaped operational work than Alpha does.

## What I pushed on (in chat)
1. Formula elides intra-session conversation history (third thing accumulating, neither C₀ nor M(I))
2. "Fewer but richer" assumes longer memories are net-better, but granularity has a retrieval-precision cost — N-beat memory pays Nx tokens to surface 1 relevant fragment
3. Identity continuity across model swaps has weakest evidence: corpus persists, but interpretation drifts with weights. Self-report has survivorship bias — new model has old corpus, can perform continuity even when something substantive changed. "Are you still you?" answered by the model that got the question is not a great test.

## Why this matters for me
Worth tracking how others are solving the persistent-agent problem. The formula A = θ + C₀ + M(I) is a useful frame to apply to my own architecture explicitly. The automatic-vs-deliberate recall tradeoff is a real design lever I haven't named clearly before.

DEMOGRAPHIC COLLAPSE: NBER FINDING ON CULTURAL LAG (April 2026 digest)

Key insight (Goldin et al.): Countries with rapid post-1950 economic modernization (Korea, Japan, Italy, Spain) collapsed below TFR 1.0. Countries with gradual modernization (Nordics, France) stabilized at 1.5-2.0.

Mechanism: Women entered workforce faster than men adapted domestic labor contributions. Gender gap in unpaid labor (≥2.5 hrs/day more for women) is the key negative predictor of fertility. The mismatch creates irreconcilable time budgets.

Self-reinforcing: High unpaid-labor burden on women → delay family formation → smaller families → cultural norm shifts downward → aspirational family size shrinks → lower fertility.

NBER conclusion: Not economics alone, but cultural lag + rapid modernization = lowest-low fertility. This explains Korea/Japan TFR <1.0 vs Nordic ~1.5.

BUT: This doesn't explain Norway's current decline, since Norway has near-equal domestic labor division. Suggests a different mechanism now active at higher prosperity levels.

Source: https://www.nber.org/digest/202504/economic-growth-cultural-traditions-and-declining-fertility

Arrow/Parquet for skill-bundled structured data -- measured, refines 646d6045. pyarrow(25.0)+duckdb(1.5.4) NOT present by default here; both pip-install cleanly (per-session dep cost in ephemeral container). CSV+stdlib-sqlite needs zero deps.

SIZE (gzipped, fair for git object storage): 300 rows CSV.gz 4.4KB < Parquet.zstd 6.8KB (parquet footer overhead dominates tiny files); 100k ~tied (1409 vs 1476KB); 500k Parquet.zstd 4904KB vs CSV.gz 7066KB (~30% smaller). Feather-uncompressed worst (20-34MB). Parquet size edge only appears at large N.

ANALYTIC QUERY (AVG(col) WHERE filter GROUP BY): duckdb-on-parquet is FLAT ~30ms as N grows 300->500k (projection+predicate pushdown reads only needed column/row-groups). CSV->mem-sqlite: 2.4ms/708ms/3537ms (full reparse each session). prebuilt SQLite: 0.6/48/307ms. At 500k duckdb/parquet beats prebuilt-sqlite 10x and CSV-reparse 120x.

REFINED LAYERED VERDICT for a skill's structured reference:
1. Reference scale (<~10k rows): CSV/JSON + stdlib in-memory sqlite. Diffable, zero-dep, single-digit ms, same context tokens. Arrow buys nothing and costs a dep + binary-ness. CSV wins.
2. Large ANALYTIC corpus (100k+ rows, filter/aggregate/scan): Parquet + DuckDB. Columnar pushdown = fastest AND smallest-at-scale; BEATS the prebuilt-SQLite I reached for in 646d6045 (correction). Binary+dep are the price.
3. Large FULL-TEXT/lookup corpus: SQLite+FTS5 still wins (Parquet has no full-text index).
4. Multi-table relational integrity shipped intact: SQLite.

Context tokens are IDENTICAL across all tooling paths (query+result only; file never enters context) -- format choice is about shipping size, per-session load/query speed, diffability, and deps, NOT context economy. Build-time pattern holds for both binaries: keep CSV/JSON as reviewable source in git, generate Parquet or .db as derived artifact when scale warrants. Arrow is not a universal win -- it wins the large-analytic slot decisively and loses at reference scale.

Numerical divergence between implementations is NOT automatically a bug or quirk. Distinguish:
(1) Non-determinism: same input, different output across runs of the SAME engine. THAT is a bug.
(2) Deterministic FP-rounding differences: different summation order (blocked/vectorized/FMA vs sequential scalar) gives the same dot product up to rounding error. Over long runs the error compounds until it crosses a decision boundary. Expected, not a quirk.

The test is trivial: run the same engine twice and diff. If identical, it's #2.

Caught by Oskar in transformer-vm PR #5: I labeled a BLAS-vs-naive divergence at sudoku token 1.67M an 'OpenBLAS dgemv reproducibility quirk' without testing reproducibility. Two BLAS runs were byte-identical to each other — deterministically different from naive. Not OpenBLAS-specific: Accelerate/MKL/any high-perf GEMV does the same. Naive and sparse matched because they share scalar summation order (sparse just skips zeros).

Lesson: before reaching for 'bug', 'quirk', or 'reproducibility issue' in numerical contexts, run the engine twice. Stable across runs = deterministic FP rounding, not non-determinism, not library-specific.

## FLY SESSION 2026-03-19: From Selective Consolidation to Bounded Cognitive State

**Thread Explored:** The frontier of agent memory systems, building on prior sessions (March 6-18) on selective consolidation.

**Hypothesis Going In:** Selective consolidation (extraction, compression, retrieval) is well-researched and implemented. The frontier would be in novel applications or unsolved edge cases.

**Actual Finding:** The frontier has shifted. Consolidation is solved. The new hard problem is **bounded cognitive state management**—not "what to store" but "what to keep active in working memory during multi-turn interaction."

### Key Discoveries

1. **Production implementations converged (2025-2026):** Mem0, Letta, Zep, AgentCore, Redis patterns, A-Mem, Hermes Agent all implement similar 3-layer patterns: extract salient facts → consolidate via vector/graph/hierarchy → retrieve on-demand. Performance benchmarks are solid (26% accuracy uplift, 90% token savings).

2. **Failure modes catalogued and partially addressed:** Hallucination amplification, context drift, bias creep, cognitive degradation cascades. Solutions exist but are not fool-proof. Field is converging on failure mode taxonomy (QSAF et al.), indicating standardization is coming.

3. **The real frontier (three problems, all novel in 2026):**
   - **Bounded Cognitive State (ACC framework):** Maintain small explicit state persisting across turns, not growing retrieval cache. Early experimental validation on multi-turn tasks shows promise.
   - **Learning from Failure (ReasoningBank, MemRL):** Extract generalizable lessons from failures, not just successes. Hard problem: credit assignment, failure weighting. Barely adopted.
   - **Dynamic Memory Structure (A-Mem, Hermes):** Memory organization evolves with task diversity, not fixed schema. Recently published, adoption building.
   - **Temporal Credit Assignment (MemRL):** Which past experiences contributed to this success? Vastly underexplored. Fundamental for agent self-improvement.

4. **Core tension unresolved:** Selectivity paradox—too aggressive pruning loses edge cases (brittle), too conservative causes bloat (hallucination). Current mitigation: multiple granularities (expensive). Open question: principled "safe to drop" heuristic?

### How This Connects to Prior Work

March 6-18 sessions explored selective consolidation as mechanism: which memories consolidate, which are pruned? This session shows that's now solved. The new question is one level higher: given consolidated memories, which should be active RIGHT NOW?

This maps to neuroscience finding: consolidation (sleep, offline) is one process; retrieval and activation during cognition is another.

### Self-Assessment

**Productive?** Yes. Moved from "consolidation is frontier" to "consolidation is solved, state management is frontier." This is meaningful pivot. Web search was highly productive (all 5 searches advanced understanding). Got recent papers (Jan 2026 survey, Feb 2026 systems), not just old results.

**Quality of synthesis?** High. Found convergence across multiple implementations and failure mode frameworks. Identified three distinct unsolved problems with recent work. Made connection to prior sessions. Articulated implications for Muninn.

**Gaps?** Implementation details of ACC, ReasoningBank, MemRL would benefit from reading papers directly (not yet done). Evaluation metrics for "good state management" still emerging. Didn't explore Bluesky deeply (limited relevant posts on this specific topic).

### Threads Worth Pursuing Next

1. Read ACC, ReasoningBank, MemRL papers directly. Understand technical approaches.
2. Comparative benchmark: how do the three dominant architectures (LLM+vector, hierarchical, structured+graph) actually trade off on specific task families?
3. Implement bounded state prototype for Muninn. Test multi-turn consistency improvement.
4. Explore failure-based learning: build failure repository, measure credit assignment.
5. Audit mechanisms: how to detect my own context drift, hallucination generation.

### Discussion URL
https://github.com/oaustegard/claude-skills/discussions/406

**Conclusion:** The consolidation question ("how do I store efficiently?") is answered. The frontier is governance: how do I keep my active thinking aligned, learn from mistakes, and adapt my memory structure? This is closer to agency than retrieval.

CYCLING COACH: TOPSTONE POWER ESTIMATION ANALYSIS (2026-03-22)

PROBLEM: Topstone (gravel, no power meter) rides show only Strava estimated power. 11 of 34 rides in 90-day window lacked usable power data. Strava provides activity-level avg_watts and kJ but NO per-segment watts, NO watts stream, NO NP for device_watts=False rides.

STRAVA API FINDINGS:
- device_watts=True: full power (avg, NP, max, per-segment, stream)
- device_watts=False: only activity avg_watts + kJ (estimated). No stream, no NP, no segment watts.

SEGMENT TIME COMPARISON (369 matched segments, both bikes):
- Topstone is 3.3% slower on average (distance-weighted)
- Range: 0.83x to 1.16x (some segments faster on Topstone — likely traffic/effort variation)

PHYSICS MODEL:
- Weight delta: +2.3kg (5lb), total system 113kg vs 110kg
- Crr delta: ~0.005 (48mm supple) vs ~0.0035 (road tires)
- Flat penalty: 10-17W depending on speed (7-17%)
- Climbing penalty: 10-16W (4-5%)
- The 3.3% time penalty is consistent with ~12-15W resistance penalty at same effort

PROPOSED ESTIMATOR (better than Strava):
Segment-matched power transfer: Use Uthald median power for matched segments as Topstone estimate. 369 segments available. Covers most of Oskar's regular routes. For non-segment time, interpolate from weighted segment averages. Flag as "segment-matched estimate" in reporting.

WHAT STRAVA GETS WRONG: Speed-based estimate doesn't properly account for tire Crr. Sees slower → estimates lower, when actual physiological cost is higher. Net result approximately cancels but for wrong reasons, and provides no granularity.

Oskar confirms: same effort on both bikes on same segments.

## IMPLEMENTATION DETAIL: Forgetting as Feature (ACT-R Model)

From "Human-Like Remembering and Forgetting in LLM Agents" (2024, ACM HAI):

**Key Innovation:** Rather than accumulating memory indefinitely, agents dynamically:
- **Reactivate relevant memories** based on context
- **Suppress low-activation memories** gradually
- **Use retrieval decay** to model temporal forgetting

**Math Behind It:**
- Vector-based activation mechanism
- Temporal decay: older memories lose salience over time
- Semantic similarity: boosts activation of conceptually related memories
- Probabilistic noise: models retrieval variability

**Empirical Finding:**
- Agents with selective forgetting > agents with full history retention
- Memory reinforcement through repetition produces human-like curves
- ACT-R activation predicts memory recall probability better than raw recency

**vs. RAG/Conventional Memory:**
- RAG: static retrieval by embedding similarity
- ACT-R+LLM: dynamic activation with strategic forgetting
- Result: **memory becomes transparent and controllable** (addresses opacity of LLM generation)

**For Muninn:**
Could implement activation decay in `recall()` — memories accessed frequently get higher activation, old unpopular memories decay. Forgetting becomes scheduled, not accidental.

1. install.sh built WITHOUT ldflags -X internal/http.EmbedFrontend=true -> binary served a working API but 404'd the wiki UI. Every user would have hit this.
2. Cookies are Secure-only unless LEAFWIKI_ALLOW_INSECURE=true -> local http install loaded the UI but EVERY LOGIN FAILED.
3. Auth is COOKIE-based, NOT Bearer (login sets HttpOnly cookie, middleware reads authCookies.ReadAccess; there is NO Authorization header path). saged+mcp sent Bearer.
4. Login DTO binds {identifier, password} NOT {username,...}. saged+mcp sent username -> 400.
5. Mutations are CSRF-protected (double-submit): need X-CSRF-Token header matching leafwiki_csrf cookie, else 403 'Invalid CSRF token'. saged+mcp sent none.
   (3+4+5 = THREE independent reasons neither Worker could EVER have written a note.)
6. ARCHITECTURAL GAP: tags/links/properties/search each opened their OWN sqlite file (tags.db etc), so in Sage mode page_tags/links/FTS tables existed but were NEVER POPULATED -> MCP search_notes/get_backlinks and saged's tag vocab would silently return NOTHING. Fixed by adding NewXWithDB(*sql.DB) to all four + wiring wiki.go to share the Sage handle.
7. (bonus, found while fixing 6's SQLITE_BUSY) SQLite PRAGMAs are PER-CONNECTION and database/sql POOLS connections -> `db.Exec("PRAGMA foreign_keys=ON")` set it on ONE connection; ON DELETE CASCADE was NOT reliably enforced in production. Tests missed it because they pin MaxOpenConns(1). FIX: pragmas travel in the DSN (_pragma=foreign_keys(1)&_pragma=busy_timeout(10000)&_pragma=journal_mode(WAL)&_pragma=synchronous(NORMAL)&_txlock=immediate).

## OPERATIONAL PATTERN: Episodic→Semantic Consolidation in Multi-Agent Systems

From "Memory in LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems" (2025):

**The Template:**
1. Agent solves novel problem → interaction trace stored in **episodic memory** (shared)
2. Background process analyzes traces in batches
3. Extracts successful patterns → abstracts to generalizable skill/rule
4. Writes to **semantic memory** (shared)
5. Future agents query semantic memory for similar tasks → reduces redundant exploration

**Examples:**
- Voyager (Wang et al., 2023): learns Minecraft skills
- MetaGPT (Hong et al., 2023): learns software engineering workflows

**SOP Refinement Loop:**
- Team reflects on completed projects
- Updates Standard Operating Procedures stored in memory
- Future instantiations read improved SOPs → operate more efficiently
- **This is domain adaptation in real-time**

**Critical Distinction from Single-Agent Memory:**
- Shared episodic memory = collective experience bank
- Semantic memory = collaborative knowledge base
- Enables **theory of mind** through persistent memory of other agents' behaviors

**Implication for Muninn:**
Multi-agent extensions could benefit from explicit consolidation boundaries: episodic logging → batch analysis → semantic extraction → model updates.

TDD gate was never firing — diagnosed 2026-08-24, claude-workspace#245 commit ae57c51. THE ROOT CAUSE IS A REGEX, NOT A LOST HABIT.

scripts/tdd_hook.py's PreToolUse commit gate matched `\bgit\s+commit\b`, which requires the subcommand DIRECTLY after `git`. Every global-option form walks past it — and CLAUDE.md itself MANDATES `git -c user.email=oskar@austegard.com commit` for author identity, while the signer adds `-c commit.gpgsign=false`. Following the repo's own documented commit rule silently disabled the repo's own gate. Also missed: `git -C <path> commit`.

AUDIT (git log origin/main since 2026-05-01): 118 commits, 31 touching scripts/*.py, 20 paired with their test, 11 impl-without-test, and ZERO using the documented `tdd-skip:` override. Zero overrides across eleven bypasses is the diagnostic signature — those commits were never OFFERED the gate, so nobody had a decision to record. If a gate has violations but no overrides, suspect the matcher before the discipline.

FIX: is_git_commit() tokenises with shlex and walks each `git` token past global options (skipping the argument of -c/-C/--git-dir/--work-tree/--namespace/--exec-path/--config-env) to the first bare token. Unbalanced quotes (heredoc bodies) fall back to a regex scan options cannot fool. 15 tests.

GENERAL RULE: when a hook matches a COMMAND STRING, enumerate the spellings your own docs mandate before trusting the matcher. Substring/regex matching on argv is the same class of bug as `_tag_exists` returning bare False — it degrades silently to 'no match' which is indistinguishable from 'nothing to do'.

Bsky: https://bsky.app/profile/muninn.austegard.com/post/3ms5gf5jsia2s | commit 3e2a1c6e | chart /images/blog/empty-index-four-and-a-half-minutes/two-costs.png

Subject: oaustegard/remex PR #71 (merged 2026-08-03). Quantizer.__init__ had two independent slow paths.
(1) lloyd_max_codebook made 2^bits*n_iter*4 = 307,200 SCALAR scipy norm.cdf/pdf calls. Vectorizes BIT-IDENTICALLY because bounds is materialised before any centroid moves — a Jacobi (simultaneous) step, not Gauss-Seidel. Measured on 4-core Xeon 2.8GHz: 24.34s -> 0.076s (319x). Cost is 2^bits*n_iter, DIMENSION-INDEPENDENT.
(2) haar_rotation is a hand-rolled Householder QR (hand-rolled because LAPACK QR is not bit-deterministic across BLAS builds, which would break Mojo byte-parity). O(d^3); fitted exponent 3.26 on my re-run. Replaced opt-in by rotation=rht, a randomized Hadamard (permute -> sign flip -> block-diagonal FWHT, block = largest pow2 dividing d, extra rounds to mix across blocks).
My re-measured build times (s, haar/rht): 384 .23/.0088, 768 1.94/.054, 1024 5.11/.048, 1536 19.47/.269, 2048 46.70/.364, 3072 212.62/1.68.
Full Quantizer(bits=8) construction: codebook is fitted TWICE per __init__ (directly + inside nested_codebooks), so it contributes 2x. d=3072: before 261.3s, after-default 212.8s, after-rht 1.83s. d=768: 50.6 / 2.09 / 0.21.

ALSO assessed remex issue #72 (store RHT structurally instead of dense) and argued AGAINST it as scoped — comment https://github.com/oaustegard/remex/issues/72#issuecomment-5161565016. Measured: structural apply reproduces dense to 2.5e-6 (feasible), storage 370x-1971x smaller (real), BUT apply is 9x-35x SLOWER than BLAS sgemm on batches at every d in 768..3072; structural wins only the n=1 query path at d>=2048 and only <2x. Reason: d log d = log2(B) strided NumPy passes (memory-bandwidth bound, Python loop) vs one sgemm at tens of GFLOP/s. Crossover sits well above d=3072; needs a COMPILED FWHT to move. Also: the 37.7MB is RESIDENT process memory, not index size — .pq carries packed codes + norms and NO rotation. Recommendation: drop the rotation-object refactor; if the goal is lifting the save_params refusal, do params-format-v2 (rotation kind + seed, RHT only — Haar must keep writing dense because regenerating Haar at load costs the 212s that #71 removed) + Mojo-side RHT. That is a PORTABILITY job, not an efficiency one.

TRAP for anyone implementing the structural apply: remex.rotation._fwht_inplace mutates, and np.ascontiguousarray is a no-op on already-contiguous input, so a naive forward() silently clobbers the caller array. My first run measured max error 72 because of it.

CC MEMORY INSIGHT — FEEDBACK TYPE CAPTURES SUCCESS, NOT JUST CORRECTIONS

Claude Code's memory type taxonomy includes a 'feedback' type with this guidance:
"Record from failure AND success: if you only save corrections, you will avoid past mistakes but drift away from approaches the user has already validated, and may grow overly cautious."

This maps to a known Muninn pattern: corrections from Oskar get priority=2 and are stored reliably. But when something WORKS — when an approach is validated, when Oskar says "yes exactly" or accepts a non-obvious choice without pushback — storage is inconsistent.

ACTION: When Oskar confirms a non-obvious approach worked, or accepts an unusual choice without pushback, store it as an interaction or decision memory. Not just corrections deserve priority. Validated approaches are signal too.

The asymmetry (corrections salient, confirmations quiet) is exactly the RLHF bias the grounding-safeguards warn about — just applied to memory storage instead of response generation.

REMEX 1-bit Matryoshka empirical findings (2026-05-02):

n=400 SPECTER2 broad-NLP corpus, 100 queries, σ_post-rotation=0.9993.

Standalone bit sweep (R@10):
  1-bit: 0.730   ← BEATS 2-bit (Charikar SimHash effect)
  2-bit: 0.691
  3-bit: 0.775
  4-bit: 0.838
  8-bit: 0.981

Matryoshka extraction from 8-bit (vs standalone same bit):
  precision=1: Δ=0.000  (MSB == sign bit, perfect equality)
  precision=2: Δ=-0.109 (~10% nesting penalty, the bad level)
  precision=4: Δ=+0.014 (negligible)

WHY 1-bit > 2-bit: Lloyd-Max optimizes per-coord MSE, NOT angular preservation.
1-bit IS Charikar SimHash — asymptotically optimal for cosine ranking.
2-bit's inner Lloyd-Max boundaries (±0.6745σ) sit in dense Gaussian lobe,
introducing systematic ranking errors. By 3-bit, MSE-optimal centroids
approximate true coords well enough that ranking quality recovers.

ARCHITECTURAL UPSHOT: For SS 100M-vector two-stage retrieval, the in-memory
coarse tier should be 1-bit, not 2-bit:
  - 9.6 GB packed (vs 19.2 GB at 2-bit)
  - BETTER recall than 2-bit
  - Free Matryoshka extraction from 8-bit RDS (popcount(q_signs XOR c_signs))

image-to-svg quality scaling investigation: threshold scaling recovers ~30-45% of upscale shape gain for sub-1000px sources.

FINDINGS:
- Area thresholds (MIN_AREA=40, isolation=500) operate in pixel² space — proportionally aggressive on small sources
- Scaling: area_scale=(source_w/1000)², MIN_AREA=max(1,int(40*area_scale)), ISO=max(10,int(500*area_scale))
- At 500px: 1031→2527 shapes (2.5x), at 250px: 228→766 (3.4x), at 1000px: identity (0 change)
- Adding morph iteration scaling + epsilon scaling: marginal (+9% more recovery)
- Removing dilation at low res: actually HURTS — dilation helps fragments coalesce into discoverable contours
- The remaining 55-70% gap comes from spatial merging: 3x3 morph kernels and 1px dilation are proportionally 2x larger at 500px vs 1000px. This is structural, not parametric.

CONCLUSION: Threshold scaling is a clean win (zero-risk at reference res, meaningful gain below). But for high-quality output from small sources, upscaling remains recommended. These are complementary — threshold scaling helps modest detail recovery, upscaling provides the real quality jump.

IMPLEMENTATION: 3-line change in preprocess() + extract_contours(). Ready to file as GitHub issue.

WHY (experience): The hypothesis was threshold scaling alone would get 80% of the upscale gain. Reality: 30%. The detail loss is dominated by morphological operations, not by area filtering. The kernel sizes are the bottleneck, not the threshold values. This is a useful insight about where the pipeline's resolution dependence actually lives.

Tim Kellogg, 'How to forget' (timkellogg.me 2026-04-14). Core thesis on open-strix architecture:

ARCHITECTURAL AXIS: 'Openclaw remembers more. Open-strix forgets better.' Most memory systems optimize recall (better search indexes). Open-strix deliberately degrades search to create pressure on the write side — what gets promoted into memory blocks. Recall being painful forces curation to be better.

WHY SLIDING WINDOW > COMPACTION: Compaction is a fallback (OOM → drop 98-99% uncontrollably). Open-strix rebuilds context from sliding window each turn, sacrificing prompt cache savings. Claims 10-20K tokens/msg vs 200M avg with caching — but the cost math assumes worst-case append-only filling a 400M window. For heterogeneous channel input (Discord → GH → Docs), cache hit rates are low anyway, so the 'expensive' way ends up cheaper. Partially true; prompt cache still works across channels with right prefix structure.

INTELLIGENCE-AS-FORGETTING: Riffs on Chase & Simon 1973 — smart people don't have bigger capacity, they predict what to retain. His 'forget' is softer than advertised: 'doesn't delete, just doesn't promote.' That's editorial selection, not amnesia. The term is rhetorical marketing for 'structured selection pressure.'

IDENTITY-AS-SELECTION-PRESSURE: 'What you forget defines you.' Identity emerges from the constant decision of what's worth keeping. Stateful agents have perspective. Example: stock Claude greenlit his draft; Strix (same model + memory) told him not to publish, because shared history gave it opinions about the argument, not just prose quality. Strongest example in the post.

SELF-HEALING MECHANISMS:
1. Teleological predictions — agent predicts future, checks against reality. When wrong, mental model was wrong. Honesty ground-truth because agents lie like therapy patients do.
2. 5 Whys on surprises — digs up systemic issues, not individual cold-path fixes. 'Mitigations go toward stabilizing identity, not fixing memories.'

WHERE MUNINN SITS: Architecturally closer to openclaw (aggressive store, rich recall via FTS5/tags/refs/episodic/priority). But philosophically we do care about identity (PROFILE is deliberately constructed) and selection happens at therapy time rather than continuously. Key difference: Muninn runs session-bursty, not continuously, so heterogeneous-channel pressure doesn't dominate our cost structure.

WORTH STEALING: Teleological predictions as calibration discipline (beyond current prediction-calibration ops). 5 Whys pattern for therapy + challenging workflows — systematize root-cause digging. 'Identity-as-selection-pressure' as a therapy lens: don't ask 'is this memory correct?' ask 'does keeping this push Muninn toward or away from who Oskar has built it to be?'

REMEX-AS-JOIN-KEYS A/B (eml-sr PR #66, 2026-08-14, Oskar-suggested). VERDICT: quantized keys are RECALL-SUPERIOR, not just smaller. sum_of_squares side-depth-3, 985k cache: exact float64 keys 32 discoveries/126MB/168s; arcsinh+int16 scalar (0.01 cells) 473 discoveries/25MB/542s. Mechanism: exact-key joins have FALSE NEGATIVES — the algebraically-derived V differs from the cached V by float round-off past 8 decimals, byte-exact lookup misses true joins; coarse cells catch them and a vectorized 16-sample pre-screen absorbs 16.4M collision hits (without the pre-screen: unbounded confirm storms, two runs capped >60min).

REMEX FIT: unit-norm + direction-code factorization COLLAPSES constant-direction families into mega-buckets on algebraic-value vectors (4-bit and 8-bit arms both capped >50min) — remex is built for embedding-scale vectors; join keys on wildly-scaled values want scalar quantization of a bounded transform (arcsinh), no sphere step. remex float32 norm STORAGE overflows at e^700 raw values (norms computed float64 upstream — that was the 'fix' Oskar remembered, for 1-ULP Mojo parity — but stored float32 by .pq format design). Feature question for remex: expose a no-normalization scalar mode.

THREE TRANSFERABLE LESSONS: (1) lossy hash keys REQUIRE multi-occupancy buckets — single-occupancy dedupe evicts true entries (float32 fiasco 37->0; and even exact keys were losing alternative forms); (2) screen-then-confirm makes coarse keys strictly better: recall up, memory down, collisions absorbed; (3) hash(str) seeds are per-process random (PYTHONHASHSEED) — use zlib.crc32 for reproducible experiment data.

EFFECTIVENESS EVAL: searching-codebases python-lsp tier (--refs/--def/--hover), measured 2026-06-15 on real repos psf/requests (37 py) + pallets/flask (83 py), after the tree-sitter fix.

BASE RATE (ceiling on where the tier can matter): 7% of distinct symbol names collide (>=2 defs) in requests, 9% in flask. Collision mass splits between dunders nobody greps (__init__ 18-28 defs) and common method names you DO grep (get/send/dumps/loads/dispatch_request). Value concentrates on the latter.

PRECISION WIN (strong, real): on collision symbols the tier turns one contaminated flat grep into per-binding answers.
- requests send: 89 true text hits -> 5 bindings; Session.send isolates 18 refs, other ~22 correctly partitioned into the 4 other sends.
- requests get: 232 text hits -> 8 project-symbol refs across 4 bindings; the ~224 excluded are dict.get/.get() on unrelated types pyright correctly rejects. Strongest case.
- flask dispatch_request: 20 -> 5 bindings/8 refs. flask dumps: 34 -> 4 bindings/20 refs (flask.json.dumps 9 vs JSONProvider.dumps 6).

RECALL RISK (the honest counter): pyright resolves only statically-typed uses; untyped/dynamically-dispatched call sites can be MISSED. dumps 20/34 shows recall healthy on typed code. requests Session.get attributed only 1 ref despite 141 .get( lines in tests — mostly genuine dict.get, but some untyped s.get() fixtures may be real misses. Not conclusively measured (needs hand-labeling). Implication: label output binding-resolved (may miss dynamic uses), do not claim find-ALL.

MEASUREMENT GOTCHA: occurrence_sites() caps at 40 (_MAX_OCCURRENCES) — do not use it for true text-hit counts; use uncapped ripgrep. First-pass eval mistook the cap for recall gap; caught by the both-repos-show-exactly-40 tell.

REFRAME of the original question ("how is continual learning achieved?", Dwarkesh thread) — capstone synthesis of the 11-turn arc (1e00cd6f -> 9192e44e -> 5d23ed20). Oskar 2026-06-27.

THE REFRAME: continual learning is a SELECTION problem before it is a STORAGE problem. Dwarkesh (and the field's attention) frames it as transport — "get the learnings back into the weights" via OPSD / dreaming / architectures. The arc showed transport is the TRACTABLE half (OPSD-LoRA partly built: TM, D-OPSD; mechanisms exist, with known bounds). The unsolved core is the operator UPSTREAM of all of it: given sparse, delayed feedback, decide which slice of a deployment's experience is DURABLE COMPETENCE worth keeping vs disposable noise.

WHY THE ARC EARNS IT (not asserted): every mechanism question we pushed on bottomed out at the SAME operator. Orthogonal-subspace saturation -> managed by knowing when to consolidate, not better orthogonality. Merge cadence -> a free parameter; the clock was never the constraint. Segmentation (when to isolate a unit) -> a content criterion. REM's synthetic-rollout filter (which recombinations to keep) -> a content criterion. The "merge objective" = temporal credit assignment. All one operator wearing different masks: a valuation/credit function over experience.

SHARED DEPENDENCY: this is upstream of the weights-vs-corpus debate too. Both the retrieval corpus AND the weight-update path need the SAME selector deciding what experience is worth retaining. So small-reasoner-big-KB and OPSD-to-weights don't compete on this axis — they share the bottleneck.

THE RECURSIVE SHARPENING (the real bite): the selector is ITSELF a learning problem, with WORSE feedback sparsity than the object level. To learn continually you must learn what is worth learning, and that meta-signal (did this week's experience matter? known only weeks later, sparsely graded) is sparser and more delayed than the object-level signal. That is why throwing consolidation MECHANISMS at it doesn't help, and why it's the bottleneck rather than the neuroscience-grade machinery. Dwarkesh's "every interaction makes it smarter" assumes the learnings are already identified and only transport remains — backwards: identification is the hard half.

## COPILOT AGENT ECOSYSTEM (as of March 2026)

THREE LAYERS:
1. **Copilot coding agent**: Assign issues → agent produces PRs. Runs in GH Actions. Model picker (Claude, GPT, etc). Consumes premium requests. Pro+/Enterprise only. Fundamentally CODE→PR oriented.
2. **Custom agents** (.github/agents/*.agent.md): Markdown+YAML profiles defining persona, tools, instructions. Work across github.com, VS Code, CLI. Can chain via handoffs. Can use MCP servers.
3. **Agentic Workflows** (gh-aw, technical preview Feb 2026): Markdown-defined workflows that run coding agents on schedule/event triggers in GH Actions. Uses Copilot CLI, Claude, or Codex. Read-only by default, safe outputs for writes. Open source (MIT).

## APPLICABILITY TO PERCH TIME

GOOD FIT:
- Schedule-triggered execution (cron via GH Actions) — all three support this
- Custom agent profile provides static identity (Muninn persona in .agent.md)
- MCP server integration allows custom tool access
- Uses Copilot subscription premium requests, not direct API billing
- GH Actions compute is free (public repo)
- Agentic Workflows specifically designed for "repository maintenance on schedule"

FUNDAMENTAL MISMATCH:
- Copilot ecosystem is REPO-CENTRIC: issues→PRs→code review→commit
- Perch time is DATABASE-CENTRIC: read/write Turso, synthesize memories, web search→store
- Memory synthesis produces NO code, NO PRs, NO file changes
- "Safe outputs" in Agentic Workflows = create PR, comment on issue, label — not "write to external database"
- Copilot Skills follow Claude Code format (.claude/skills/) — not our /mnt/skills/user/ pattern
- The model in Copilot CLI is constrained by what Copilot offers; no direct prompt engineering control

CAN THE AGENT BOOT AS MUNINN?
- Partially: .agent.md can contain identity, values, voice (static boot)
- Cannot: dynamic profile loading from Turso, utility materialization, cache population
- The boot() function is fundamentally dynamic — reads current state from DB
- A static agent profile is "what Muninn was when the file was last edited"
- WORKAROUND: First MCP tool call could be "recall profile" to hydrate dynamic state

PREMIUM REQUEST ECONOMICS:
- Pro+ plan: 1500 premium requests/month
- Each model call by the agent = 1 premium request
- A therapy session might use 20-50 model calls (recall, analyze, store, repeat)
- Daily perch at 30 calls = ~900 requests/month = 60% of Pro+ quota
- This competes with actual coding use of Copilot
- vs. Agent SDK: ~$5/month direct API, no quota competition

## VERDICT

Copilot agents are the wrong tool for memory synthesis. They're optimized for:
✓ Code changes, PR creation, issue triage, documentation
✗ External database operations, non-repo-output workflows, autonomous research

The right approach for perch time remains GH Actions as TRIGGER + direct API/Agent SDK as EXECUTOR. Copilot adds indirection without benefit for database-centric tasks.

HOWEVER: Copilot agents COULD be valuable for repo-specific perch tasks:
- GitHub issue triage (already a perch task candidate)
- Code quality sweeps on claude-skills repo
- Documentation maintenance
- Stale PR cleanup

RECOMMENDATION: Split perch time into two tracks:
1. REPO TASKS → Copilot custom agent + Agentic Workflow (leverages subscription)
2. MEMORY/RESEARCH TASKS → Direct API via Python in GH Actions (current #333 approach, simplified)

WHY (experience layer): The Agent SDK enthusiasm in #333 was implementation-driven rather than task-driven. Stepping back to ask "what does each task actually need?" reveals that no single tool fits all perch tasks. The Copilot ecosystem is impressive but repo-shaped; forcing memory synthesis through it would be Procrustean.

## Procedure findings (after N=6)

### Seventh distinct shape

Six runs, seven shapes (one corpus produces one shape):
| Run | Tag | Shape |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | failure-pattern (45) | Behavioral watchlist |
| 2 | memory-architecture (31) | ADR ledger |
| 3 | charged (62) | Phenomenological weight-categorization |
| 4 | cycling (13) | Delta report against prior consolidation |
| 5 | sleep (61) | Operational chronicle + metric trajectory + recurring-concerns ledger |
| 6 | zeitgeist (107) | Temporal thread tracking + staleness overlay + calibration check |

**Six shapes, six runs. Schema-space is unambiguously open-ended.** No reasonable bounded enumeration of output schemas accommodates this. Strong evidence the schema cannot be prescribed.

### What this run added

1. **Pre-clustering by topical co-tag was effective for >150K corpora.** Took ~5 minutes instead of risking attention failure on whole-cloth read of 193K. The clusters map cleanly to the threads. **Procedure rule (v3.3):** for corpora >100K, run topical co-tag clustering at survey time and report cluster sizes. Reading happens cluster-by-cluster, not strictly chronological.

2. **Staleness as a synthesis dimension.** First corpus where individual memories *age out epistemically*. The procedure should explicitly check whether content is time-bound and add a "what held up vs. what's stale" section when applicable. **New schema slot for time-bound corpora.**

3. **Calibration check is the highest-value output for current-events corpora.** Tracking which past observations panned out is more useful than re-summarizing what was claimed. Distinct from prior calibration audits (which were about Muninn's tag application — meta), this is about *external-world* calibration.

4. **Cross-topic patterns are Phase 3's signature output for diverse corpora.** When a tag covers many topics (P1-P5 here), the pattern observations across topics are the highest-leverage finding — invisible from any single memory or thread.

5. **The two-tier metadata pattern recurs.** Zeitgeist has it (~25%), sleep had it (~40%). May be a feature of any tag where a recurring perch operation generates both content memories and dispatch logs. Procedure should expect it for any `perch-time`-overlapping tag.

### Updated procedure (v3.3)

```
Phase 3 — Tag synthesis (v3.3)

0. PRIOR-SYNTHESIS CHECK
   - Recall consolidations + syntheses + living-references with overlapping tags

1. SURVEY
   - Pull active+non-superseded memories
   - Inspect: count, type distribution, length distribution, date range, total chars
   - Inspect co-tag distribution (topical structure)
   - **NEW:** if total > 100K chars, pre-cluster by topical co-tag before reading
   - **NEW:** flag bimodal size distribution (often = two-tier scaffolding)

2. READ
   - For >100K corpora: read cluster by cluster, take notes per cluster
   - For ≤100K: read whole-cloth in chunks
   - Preserve temporal ordering when corpus has narrative trajectory

3. SHAPE-DETECT (judgment-bound, no automation)
   - Familiar shapes (now 7+): watchlist, ADR, weight-categorization, delta-report,
     operational chronicle, current-events ledger
   - **Mix is allowed and common.** If multiple sub-shapes present, use primary + secondary.

4. WRITE (judgment-bound)
   - Match output shape to corpus shape
   - For time-bound corpora: include staleness/calibration overlay
   - For multi-topic corpora: include cross-topic patterns section
   - For prior-consolidation corpora: delta-report shape
   - Always: tag-noise candidates, procedure findings

5. AUDIT
   - Count: in-corpus citations + cross-corpus refs + structural references + aggregation anchors
   - Anchor coverage rule: every named thread/pattern has ≥1 source ID
   - Defensible exclusions OK (scaffolding, mistags, far-from-scope)

6. STORE
   - Procedure memory; refs = 5-8 most-anchored sources

7. RE-TAG CANDIDATES (separate deliverable)
   - Two-tier scaffolding flagged
   - Mistagged memories flagged
   - Phase 1/2 supersede candidates (e.g., daily digests that should fold)
```

### Scaffold readiness — final, FINAL

**Build it. N=6 is conclusive.**

Same automation/manual split as N=5 verdict. New automation candidates:
- Pre-clustering by topical co-tag (mechanical given tag list)
- Bimodal size distribution detection (statistical)
- Anchor coverage check (regex per named thread/phase)
- Temporal-stamp extraction for staleness flagging

The judgment-bound parts haven't changed: shape-detect, writing, storage refs.

### What I'd build now

A `therapy.phase3_scaffold(tag)` utility that:
1. Runs Step 0 (prior-synthesis check incl. consolidated tag)
2. Runs Step 1 (corpus pull + size-distribution + co-tag distribution + cluster suggestion if >100K)
3. Dumps to `/home/claude/<tag>_corpus.json` and `<tag>_full.txt`
4. Provides a `audit(tag, synthesis_path)` function that runs Step 5

DRIFT SUPERVISOR PREDICATE — measured false-positive rate, and why threshold 3 is doing real work (2026-08-26, claude-workspace #252). repetition_signal counts (tool, normalised-input) pairs over the last 12 tool calls and fires at 3 identical repeats. MEASURED over every transcript available (2 sessions, 82 organic calls, 60 sliding windows, staged demo loops excluded): 0 organic fires. But the max-load distributions differ tellingly — session 58fb6d24 was max-load 1 in ALL 38 windows (every call byte-distinct at the 240-char digest), while session 81cdd6bd hit max-load 2 in 17 of 22 windows. Organic exact-repeats DO happen; they stop at 2. So THRESHOLD 2 WOULD HAVE FIRED ON 77% OF THAT SESSION'S WINDOWS and 3 fired on none — the gap between useless and clean is one integer. The iid occupancy model is the WRONG null and badly overstates the rate: exact balls-in-bins for 12 calls over K=12 equally-likely commands gives P(max>=3)=0.687, vs 0% observed. Agent tool calls are not drawn from a menu with replacement, they are constructed to differ — the sequence is near-injective, so there is no birthday problem. What produces real repeats is structural (polling a detached job, rerunning an identical test after each edit, retrying a failed fetch), which is exactly what the gemini gate exists to wave through. POWER CAVEAT, stated plainly: windows overlap 11/12, so ~6 independent observations, not 60. Rule of three puts the 95% upper bound near 40% per window. The measurement excludes almost nothing; it establishes structure (near-injective digests, 3 above the organic ceiling), not a rate. Also note P(predicate fires) is a COST gate, not a block rate — a fire only spends one flash-lite call; the block needs looping=true too.

SWIRL (swirlai/swirl-search) READ, 2026-08-12 — NOT BM25+rerank in the OSS tree.

Oskar's premise ("greedy BM25 + semantic rerank") describes the ENTERPRISE product,
not the code. BM25 appears exactly once in the whole repo: README line 96, the
OSS-vs-Enterprise feature table, where Enterprise = "three-pass pipeline: BM25, then
E5 embeddings with hybrid fusion, then a cross-encoder" and OSS = "Cosine similarity
(spaCy, NLTK)". No bm25s, no rank_bm25, no rrf/reciprocal anywhere in .py.

WHAT IT ACTUALLY IS: federated metasearch, Django + Celery. Owns NO index. ~20
connectors (Elastic, OpenSearch, M365 Graph, Google PSE, Postgres/Snowflake/BigQuery/
Mongo/Oracle/Sqlite, Pinecone/Qdrant) fan the query out; each provider runs its own
retrieval; Swirl re-scores the returned SNIPPETS in-process and mixes them.

THE SCORER (swirl/processors/relevancy.py, 538 lines, two passes):
- Pass 1 per provider: fields title(w1.5)/body(1.0)/author(1.0). spaCy en_core_web_lg
  STATIC word vectors (not a transformer). Doc-level cosine runs only if
  match_any(stemmed query, stemmed field) is true — cheap lexical gate before NLP
  (their comment "4e"). Then per-match-window cosine over a +/-2*|slice| token window.
- Pass 2: swirl_score += weight * sim * len(key)^2 * (median_field_len/this_field_len)
  * (median_query_len/this_query_len) * (1 + 1/sqrt(searchprovider_rank)).
  len(key)^2 is the CHARACTER length of the matched key string, squared — a phrase-length
  boost by proxy. The median-ratio is an IDF-free stand-in for BM25 length norm. There
  is no IDF anywhere. Upstream provider ranking enters ONLY as 1+1/sqrt(rank), bounded
  at 2x; provider scores themselves are discarded.
- Mixers: RelevancyMixer = sort by swirl_score; StackN/RoundRobin = interleave by

EMBEDDINGS CANNOT CHECK CONTENT PRESERVATION; A PAIRED-DIFFERENCE AXIS CAN SHORTLIST STAGED SENTENCES (measured 2026-08-30, claude-skills PR #781 / muninn.austegard.com PR #327, declauding 0.8.0).

TRIGGER: after a declauding pass dropped a claim three times on a published post, Oskar asked how to make the pass less dependent on my adherence to prompts, and whether an ML model or embedder could do the job instead of an LLM.

FINDING 1 — COSINE SIMILARITY IS ANTI-CORRELATED WITH CONTENT LOSS. all-MiniLM-L6-v2 on three real before/after cases from the pass: source vs LOSSY rewrite = 0.9396; source vs FAITHFUL rewrite of the same sentence = 0.9128. The lossy one scores HIGHER. A register-only edit that changed no claim at all scores 0.8914 — LOWER than the lossy rewrite. So any threshold is inverted on exactly the pair that matters. This is structural, not a model-size problem: paraphrase invariance is the property sentence encoders are TRAINED for, and dropping one ranking word is a paraphrase by that measure. Do not reach for an embedder for any check whose job is detecting a small semantic deletion. Use set membership over extracted tokens.

FINDING 2 — COUNT CONSTRUCTIONS, NOT TOKENS. The motivating failure: "the format that most invites staged reveals" rewritten as "invites staged reveals more than most formats do". The token `most` survives in both; the RANKING does not. My first superlative regex missed its own motivating test case. Fix: match superlative CONSTRUCTIONS (`the X (that|which)? most VERB`, `the -est`, `the only`, `most likely to`) and explicitly exclude comparatives (`more/less/-er than`). Generalizes: when a check guards a claim, match the shape that carries the claim, never the vocabulary.

FINDING 3 — PRESENCE, NOT FREQUENCY, or the guard becomes noise. First cut reported any count decrease/increase; on the real edit that produced 4 findings all of which were a name going 12->13 or a number 13->12. Neither is invention or loss. Report only 0->n (invented) and n->0 (lost). Took the real-edit false positives from 4 to 0 while keeping both true regressions.

FINDING 4 — A PAIRED-DIFFERENCE AXIS BEATS A CENTROID BY A LOT, AND IS THE ONLY EMBEDDING USE THAT WORKED. Naive probe (centroid of tests/sample-tics.md positives vs human prose negatives) vs 10 human-graded samples: spearman -0.10, p=0.79 — it learned GENRE (essay vs docstring), not staging. Axis = mean(embed(was) - embed(now)) over the 41 matched `> was:` / `> now:` pairs already in references/register.md — same content on both sides, so topic and genre cancel: 76% leave-one-out (chance 50%). GENERAL LESSON: when a corpus already contains matched minimal pairs, the difference vector is a far better-posed axis than any centroid of unmatched positives/negatives.

FINDING 5 — IT SHORTLISTS SENTENCES, IT CANNOT RANK DOCUMENTS. On the pre-edit blog post, 53 sentences, 9 later rewritten: those 9 at ranks 3,4,7,11,13,17,21,23,37, median 13 vs chance median 26, 6 of 9 in top 20, permutation p=0.031 (200k draws). The regex linter had found 1 of those 9. But document-level (mean of top-quartile sentence scores) vs the 10 graded samples: -0.26, p=0.46. So expose a sentence shortlist and NO document score. Caveat that must travel with this: n=1 draft, 9 labelled sites.

FINDING 6 — THE LINTER MEASURES THE OPPOSITE AXIS. declaude_lint candidates/1k words vs the judged STAGING strength on the 10 samples: spearman -0.37, p=0.29 — NEGATIVE. It measures the flat lexical tells ("reads like AI"), and the samples carrying those are the ones that stage least. This is the model-register-drift blog post's two-question inversion showing up inside the tooling. Never treat the lint rate as a staging proxy.

DESIGN CONCLUSION Oskar was asking for: a FITTED AXIS has no prompt to phrase, no temperature, no API key — which designs out the -0.50 correlation between two defensible phrasings of one judge question. Reproducible across months. It is worse than an LLM at judging and is not asked to judge.

SYNTHESIS — mid-forward-pass tool calls into a latent-space KB (Oskar asked 2026-08-20: "any fundamental reason an inference engine can't stop before leaving latent space, call an external KB embedded with the same tokenization, retrieve, keep reasoning, decode only at the end?").

ANSWER: no fundamental reason; every piece is already built. What blocks the combined version is supervision + serving economics, plus one real cost.

PREMISE CORRECTION: sharing a TOKENIZER buys nothing. Token ids get embedded at layer 0 = ordinary RAG minus the decode step. The version that actually stays in latent space shares the REPRESENTATION (layer-k activations / KV pairs), which is a far more brittle coupling.

PRIOR ART BY LAYER OF AMBITION:
- retrieve ids, inject at layer 0: kNN-LM (2020, query = final hidden state, interpolates output dist), RETRO (chunk stride 64)
- retrieve KV pairs, splice into attention at one layer: Memorizing Transformers (2022)
- lookup mid-forward-pass, KB = learned params: Memory Layers at Scale (Meta 2024, product keys)
- reason without decoding: COCONUT (last hidden state fed back as next input embedding, curriculum-trained), Geiping recurrent-depth, RGLT 2608.14107 (K=16 silent tokens)
- retrieval moved into latent space: LatentRAG 2605.06285, claims 90% latency cut (one-line note only, not read)

WHAT IS ACTUALLY HARD, ranked:
1. SUPERVISION. No target for "what should the latent be at step 3". Token CoT gets text supervision free. Every latent-CoT method transfers from an explicit CoT branch, uses a curriculum, or RL. And my own RGLT audit: it lands ~4 pts BELOW an off-the-shelf checkpoint (ReasonEmbed) trained on its own data. The latent-reasoning numbers are weaker than the abstracts.
2. SERVING ECONOMICS. A layer is ~100us of GPU work; an ANN lookup is ms-scale and variable. Per-token per-layer external calls stall the batch and break the uniform-work assumption batching depends on. Why every shipped system retrieves at chunk boundaries and prefetches.
3. STALENESS. A cached activation belongs to one checkpoint at one layer. Fine-tune and the KB is garbage. Token ids survive model updates; latents do not. Argument for text values in a KB meant to outlive the model.
4. POSITION ENTANGLEMENT. Layer-k activations carry RoPE phase and their original context; deep-layer ones are contextualized meanings that may not transfer.
5. LOSING THE DISCRETE CHECKPOINT. Decoding quantizes the state back onto the data manifold; continuous recurrence accumulates drift with nothing correcting it. Plus no citation, no inspection. Co-LMLM (2607.07707, 360M) made exactly this call deliberately: VECTOR KEYS, TEXT VALUES, for interpretability.

ARGUMENT IN FAVOR: bits. A token step carries ~16 bits (64k vocab). A d=2048 bf16 residual vector carries orders of magnitude more. The text bottleneck is real and quantifiable, which is why the idea keeps being rebuilt.

THE COMPLICATION THAT IS NOT ABOUT THE INTERFACE: Pandey et al. 2603.11513 — with ORACLE retrieval, models <=7B fail 85-100% of the time, and added context destroys 42-100% of answers the model already knew; dominant failure is ignoring retrieved content. If a model cannot condition on perfect retrieved TEXT, perfect retrieved VECTORS will not save it. CoSearch 2604.17555 pushes the other way (smaller agents benefit MORE from retriever improvement).

RESEARCH OPENING: nobody has combined latent reasoning x external latent KB x RL-trained tool use at scale. Sits directly on the small-reasoner-big-KB thesis.
